```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(ggplot2)

# One language order for every table and figure, the order the pilot tables use. Naming
# it keeps any display from falling back on alphabetical sorting. union() keeps any
# language outside the list instead of turning it into NA.
LANG_LEVELS <- c("English", "Turkish", "Norwegian")
lang_factor <- function(x) factor(x, levels = union(LANG_LEVELS, sort(unique(x))))

# The public report is deliberately independent of participant-level pilot data.
# It uses only disclosure-reviewed derivatives that are already represented in
# the published PDF: a raster figure and aggregate sample-composition counts.
pilot_composition <- read_csv(
  "../outputs/design_summary_pilot/pilot_sample_composition.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
pilot_figure <- "../outputs/figures/pilot_acceptability_by_gender_report.png"

# Pilot-grounded (v2) summaries, aggregated on the cluster by
# scripts/aggregate_pilot.R: per-cell detection rates, the fitted pilot parameters
# and the analytic detection ceilings. Reading them here keeps every simulation
# result in the report programmatic.
jp <- read_csv("../outputs/design_summary_pilot/joint_power_pilot.csv",
               show_col_types = FALSE)
pp <- read_csv("../outputs/design_summary_pilot/pilot_params_ceilings.csv",
               show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(language = lang_factor(language)) |>
  arrange(language)

pct0  <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
num2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
num3  <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
mnum2 <- function(x) sprintf("$%.2f$", x)    # math mode, for a proper minus sign
snum2 <- function(x) sprintf("$%+.2f$", x)   # signed, in math mode
snum3 <- function(x) sprintf("$%+.3f$", x)
ppv   <- function(lang, col) pp[[col]][pp$language == lang]
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) > 1) paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1)) else
    as.character(x)
}

# Grid cells are cited only when they hold a minimum number of replicates.
MIN_REPS_V2 <- 10L
jp_a <- filter(jp, mode == "assurance", reps >= MIN_REPS_V2)

# The decision arm: the simulated studies at 70, 80 and 100 participants per language on
# which the per-language results rest, each scored for every prediction and summarised by
# scripts/aggregate_pseudo_passive.R. Every per-language rate in the text and tables is
# read from it, so the rates at those samples all rest on the same replicates. The file
# stores integer counts, and a language without a pseudo-passive carries NA in every H2
# column, so it cannot print as a test that failed.
ppd <- read_csv("../outputs/design_summary_pilot/pseudo_passive_decision_arm.csv",
                show_col_types = FALSE)
# The grid summary above counts the same replicates wherever its cell holds exactly the
# decision arm, as at 80 participants. This stops the render if a re-aggregation of
# either file leaves the two out of step.
ppd_same <- ppd |>
  inner_join(select(jp_a, language, n_participants, reps, p_h1b),
             by = c("language", "n_participants"), suffix = c("", "_jp")) |>
  filter(reps == reps_jp)
stopifnot(setequal(ppd_same$language, LANG_LEVELS),
          all(ppd_same$n_h1b == round(ppd_same$p_h1b * ppd_same$reps)))

da_reps <- unique(ppd$reps)
da_ns   <- sort(unique(ppd$n_participants))
stopifnot(length(da_reps) == 1)
da      <- function(lang, N, col) ppd[[col]][ppd$language == lang & ppd$n_participants == N]

# The populations of languages behind the pooled analysis, from
# scripts/run_klanguage_design_analysis.R on the engine in R/13_simulate_klanguage_pooled.R:
# the mean and between-language spread estimated from each of three sets of measured
# languages. The quoted rates use the set of all seven.
K_DIR <- "../outputs/design_summary_pilot/"
kpopr <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_populations_by_reading.csv"),
                  show_col_types = FALSE)
K_POPS <- c("claps_protocol", "seven", "glossa_protocol")
kpop <- function(pop, col, variant = "canonical") {
  x <- kpopr[[col]][kpopr$reading_variant == variant & kpopr$population == pop]
  stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
  x
}

# The planned number of languages: the registered minimum of 25, set by the PI on 2
# November 2026, three quarters of them, rounded, with a pseudo-passive, and the larger
# numbers the protocol shows. The convergence simulations of the single model ran with 20.
k_pp      <- function(K) as.integer(floor(0.75 * K + 0.5))
K_PLAN    <- 25L
K_PLAN_PP <- k_pp(K_PLAN)
K_MORE    <- c(30L, 35L, 40L)
K_LADDER_SIM <- 20L

# The populations for the pseudo-passive interaction, from
# scripts/run_klanguage_pseudo_passive.R, estimated from the measured languages with a
# pseudo-passive. Its three sets of languages stand in for the three above.
kpppop <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_pseudo_passive_populations.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
KPP_POPS <- c(claps_protocol = "claps_protocol", seven = "five",
              glossa_protocol = "glossa_protocol")
n_measured_pp <- kpppop$K[kpppop$population == "five"]

# The confirmatory pooled tests as registered, from scripts/run_klanguage_registered.R
# --test=onesided --known=none: the two-stage synthesis with a one-sided Bayes factor
# against a zero mean, whose hypothesis is the negative half of the normal prior on the
# mean across languages, with a half-normal(0.5) prior on tau, in simulated studies whose
# languages are all drawn from a population, since which languages will take part is not
# yet known. The quoted rates hold the population's mean and spread at their posterior
# mean and median, as a conventional power analysis does (--mode=point), at 20 to 40
# languages (--k=20,25,30,35,40), with the shares of studies ending at or below 1/10
# (--bf-bands).
kpoint <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_languages_point_bands_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(kpoint$known == "none"), all(kpoint$mode == "point"), all(kpoint$test == "onesided"),
          length(unique(kpoint$n_reps)) == 1)
# The registered tables name their sets as the two population tables above do.
KREG_POPS <- list(H1 = setNames(K_POPS, K_POPS), H2 = KPP_POPS)
kreg_row <- function(h, pop = "seven", tab = kpoint, K = if (h == "H1") K_PLAN else K_PLAN_PP) {
  x <- tab[tab$hypothesis == h & tab$population == KREG_POPS[[h]][[pop]] & tab$K == K, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1)
  x
}
kreg_rate <- function(h, pop = "seven", ...) kreg_row(h, pop, ...)$power
kreg_ci <- function(h, pop = "seven", ...) {
  x <- kreg_row(h, pop, ...)
  sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * x$power_lo, 100 * x$power_hi)
}
# Every number of languages the text quotes is in the table, and the text says that no
# study at the estimated effect ends at a Bayes factor of 1/10 or less.
stopifnot(all(c(K_PLAN, K_MORE) %in% kpoint$K[kpoint$hypothesis == "H1"]),
          all(k_pp(c(K_PLAN, K_MORE)) %in% kpoint$K[kpoint$hypothesis == "H2"]),
          all(vapply(c(K_PLAN, K_MORE), function(k) kreg_row("H1", K = k)$p_bf_low, 0) == 0),
          all(vapply(k_pp(c(K_PLAN, K_MORE)), function(k) kreg_row("H2", K = k)$p_bf_low, 0) == 0))
# A rate that falls exactly on a half, such as 3,460 of 4,000 studies, is given to one
# decimal, since sprintf() rounds halves to even and would print 86.5% as 86%.
pct_h <- function(x) {
  p2 <- 200 * x
  if (isTRUE(all.equal(p2, round(p2))) && round(p2) %% 2 == 1) sprintf("%.1f%%", p2 / 2) else pct0(x)
}
# Rates are given in whole percentages, except that a rate just below 95% that would round
# up to it is given to one decimal, rounded down, so that none reads as reaching 95%.
pct_r <- function(x) {
  if (x < 0.95 && round(100 * x) >= 95) sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(1000 * x) / 10) else pct_h(x)
}
# The rates at the larger numbers of languages, as text: H1 at K_MORE languages and H2 at
# the three quarters of them with a pseudo-passive.
more_rates <- function(h) {
  ks <- if (h == "H1") K_MORE else k_pp(K_MORE)
  vapply(ks, function(k) pct_r(kreg_rate(h, K = k)), character(1))
}
# The same tests allowing for uncertainty about the mean and spread, which each simulated
# study draws from their posterior (the assurance, --k=20,25,30,35,40 --bf-bands). The text
# quotes them once.
kunc <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_languages_bands_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(kunc$known == "none"), !"mode" %in% names(kunc), all(kunc$test == "onesided"))
# The same studies with 60 verbs per language, the fewest the protocol allows
# (--n-verbs=72,60 at 20 and 25 languages), at the estimated effect and allowing for
# uncertainty. Their 72-verb rows must be the quoted rates, and the render stops if any
# quoted rate falls by a percentage point or more, which the text rules out.
kverbs <- list(
  point = read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_verbs_languages_point_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE),
  unc = read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_verbs_languages_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                 show_col_types = FALSE))
verbs_fall <- unlist(lapply(names(kverbs), function(nm) {
  vapply(c("H1", "H2"), function(h) {
    k <- if (h == "H1") K_PLAN else K_PLAN_PP
    x <- kverbs[[nm]]
    x <- x[x$hypothesis == h & x$population == KREG_POPS[[h]][["seven"]] & x$K == k, ]
    stopifnot(nrow(x) == 2, setequal(x$n_verbs, c(60, 72)),
              isTRUE(all.equal(x$power[x$n_verbs == 72],
                               kreg_rate(h, tab = if (nm == "point") kpoint else kunc))))
    x$power[x$n_verbs == 72] - x$power[x$n_verbs == 60]
  }, numeric(1))
}))
stopifnot(all(verbs_fall < 0.01))
# Studies with no effect, a mean of zero with the estimated spread (--mode=null
# --bf-bands): the share that reaches 10 is the rate of misleading evidence.
knull <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_languages_null_bands_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                  show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(knull$mode == "null"), all(knull$test == "onesided"))
null_rate <- function(h) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * kreg_rate(h, tab = knull))

# The normal approximation to each language's analysis, from
# scripts/estimate_per_language_approximations.R, calibrated against the decision arm by
# widening its standard error by a factor k.
pla <- read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "per_language_approximations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
# The registered tests again, on the same simulated studies, with every language's
# standard error widened by that factor
# (scripts/run_klanguage_registered.R --test=onesided --known=none --se-scale=calibrated
# --k=20,25, at the estimated effect and allowing for uncertainty). The text quotes the
# largest fall of the quoted rates, and stops the render if any rose instead.
kreg_wide <- list(
  point = read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_se_scaled_languages_point_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE),
  unc = read_csv(paste0(K_DIR, "klanguage_registered_se_scaled_languages_none_known_onesided.csv"),
                 show_col_types = FALSE))
kreg_shift <- local({
  k <- unique(c(kreg_wide$point$se_scale, kreg_wide$unc$se_scale))
  stopifnot(length(k) == 1, isTRUE(all.equal(k, unique(pla$k))))
  fall <- c(vapply(c("H1", "H2"), function(h) kreg_rate(h) - kreg_rate(h, tab = kreg_wide$point), 0),
            vapply(c("H1", "H2"), function(h) kreg_rate(h, tab = kunc) - kreg_rate(h, tab = kreg_wide$unc), 0))
  stopifnot(all(fall >= 0))
  list(k = k, max_fall = max(fall))
})
# Counts below ten in words, as APA 7 asks.
num_word <- function(n) c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
                          "nine")[n]
# The agent-gender versions, taken up in Appendix B. The gender terms come from the pilot
# re-analyses in scripts/assess_gender_versions.R, a linear mixed model of the 1-to-7
# ratings with agent gender coded plus or minus a half, so they are quoted beside that
# model's own estimate of the interaction.
gve <- read_csv("../outputs/design_summary_pilot/gender_versions_gender_effects.csv",
                show_col_types = FALSE)
gvev <- function(lang, term, col = "estimate") {
  gve[[col]][gve$language == lang & gve$term == term]
}
# The gender script scales affectedness by twice its verb-level standard deviation, so a
# coefficient per standard deviation of affectedness is exactly half the fitted one.
gv_per_sd <- function(x) x / 2
GV_TERM_H1B <- "S_TypeActive:Semantics_scaled:Gender_c"
# What one agent gender for every item would do to the interaction: with the code at
# plus or minus a half, a design whose participants all see one gender shifts the slope by
# half the gender term, reported as a fraction of the slope itself.
gv_shift <- function(lang, g = 0.5) {
  abs(g * gvev(lang, GV_TERM_H1B) / gvev(lang, GV_TERM_H1B, "h1b_estimate"))
}
# Sentences in one pilot session: every verb in three sentence types and in both
# agent-gender versions. Only the verb count is read from the data.
GV_S_TYPES_ADMINISTERED <- 3L
GV_VERSIONS             <- 2L
gv_trials <- function(lang) GV_VERSIONS * GV_S_TYPES_ADMINISTERED * ppv(lang, "n_verbs")
```

`\begin{abstract}\normalsize\noindent`{=latex} CLAPS asks whether affectedness, how strongly
an event affects the person or thing it happens to, influences the acceptability of passive
sentences more than that of active ones, and whether that pattern holds across languages. The
primary hypothesis (H1) holds that the affectedness slope is steeper for passives than for
actives, and the secondary hypothesis (H2) that it is also steeper for passives than for
pseudo-passives. This report evaluates by simulation what the planned design, 80 participants per
language in at least `r K_PLAN` languages, can be expected to deliver. Both hypotheses are tested
across languages in a two-stage synthesis: each language is analysed with the planned ordinal
model, and the estimates are combined in a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis, with a one-sided
Bayes factor against the null hypothesis of no effect. Which languages will take part is not yet
known, so the simulations draw the effect of every language from a population whose mean and
spread are estimated from the seven languages measured so far: English, Turkish and Norwegian in
the CLAPS pilot, and Balinese, Hebrew, Indonesian and Mandarin in published studies. With
`r K_PLAN` languages and the effect at its estimated size, the usual basis of a power analysis,
the synthesis reaches a Bayes factor of 10 in `r pct_r(kreg_rate("H1"))` of simulated studies on
H1, and in `r pct_r(kreg_rate("H2"))` on H2 across the `r K_PLAN_PP` languages with a
pseudo-passive. With `r max(K_MORE)` languages, the rates rise to
`r pct_r(kreg_rate("H1", K = max(K_MORE)))` and `r pct_r(kreg_rate("H2", K = k_pp(max(K_MORE))))`. In the pilots, the active
interaction runs in the predicted direction in all three languages, and the pseudo-passive
interaction in English but not in Turkish. Because affectedness is a property of the verb, the
verbs bound the precision of each language's estimate.
`\end{abstract}`{=latex}

`\newpage`{=latex}

# Background

CLAPS (A Crosslinguistic Approach to Passive Semantics) asks whether the acceptability of
passive and related sentence types tracks the semantic affectedness of the patient, whether that
relationship differs by sentence type and whether it holds across languages. Affectedness, the
degree to which a patient or theme undergoes a change of state or is causally impinged upon by
the action, is a core dimension of argument structure [@dowty1991; @beavers2011]. It has long
been argued to be the semantic heart of the passive, which carries the meaning that the surface
subject is in a state or circumstance characterised by the agent having acted upon it
[@pinkerLebeauxFrost1987]. Acceptability-judgement and comprehension studies with adults in
several languages support the view that passive acceptability is semantically structured
[@ambridgeBidgoodPineRowlandFreudenthal2016; @aryawibawaAmbridge2018;
@darmasetiyawanAmbridge2022; @liuAmbridge2021; @bidgoodPineRowlandAmbridge2020;
@ambridgeArnonBekman2023].

The evidence to date spans English, Indonesian, Balinese, Hebrew and Mandarin. A Bayesian
meta-analytic synthesis of those studies finds that affectedness raises the acceptability of
passives but not of pseudo-passives [@ambridgeArnonBekman2023]. In most of the five languages,
it raises passive acceptability more than active acceptability, although the size of that
advantage varies considerably and in Balinese it runs the other way. The CLAPS pilot, run in
English, Turkish and Norwegian, adds two languages to that evidence.

Each language's data will be collected by its own team, at a sample size fixed in advance. This
report, prepared for the study's Stage 1 Registered Report, evaluates what the planned sample can
be expected to deliver. It does so through a design analysis [@schonbrodtWagenmakers2018] whose
simulated effects rest on the CLAPS pilot and on published estimates for four further languages.

# The Model and the Predictions

Each acceptability judgement is a rating from 1 to 7. The ratings are modelled with a Bayesian
cumulative-logit mixed-effects model, an ordinal model that respects the discreteness, ordering
and bounded range of rating data [@burknerVuorre2019]. Treating the same ratings as continuous
biases the regression coefficients and inflates error rates where floor or ceiling effects are
present [@liddellKruschke2018], and modelling them cumulatively recovers psycholinguistic effects
more accurately [@verissimo2021; @taylorRousseletScheepersSereno2023].

The model predicts acceptability from sentence type, affectedness and their interaction. Each
stimulus appears as an active, a passive and a pseudo-passive. In English, for example, these are
"The woman pushed the man", "The man was pushed by the woman" and "It was the man that the woman
pushed", the last a cleft that puts the patient first without the passive's morphology. Each
sentence type is treated as the same construction in every language that has it. The passive is
the reference level, and the active and the pseudo-passive are compared with it.

H1, the primary hypothesis, holds that the affectedness slope is steeper for passives than for
actives, so that the active-by-affectedness interaction is negative. H2, the secondary hypothesis,
holds that the slope is also steeper for passives than for pseudo-passives, so that the
pseudo-passive-by-affectedness interaction is negative. The passive slope itself carries no
prediction. Affectedness might raise or lower the acceptability of sentences in general, and the
theory requires only that its slope be steeper for passives, so each test compares the passive
slope with another slope, whatever their signs. H1 is
tested on the mean across all languages, and H2 on the mean across the languages with a
pseudo-passive, which the Norwegian materials do not include.

The pilot, whose sample Appendix A describes, shows the predicted pattern in English and
Norwegian (@fig-pilot). In both, the affectedness slope is positive and steepest for the passive,
and flat or slightly negative for the active, as it is for the English pseudo-passive. In
Turkish, the passive slope is also steeper than the active slope, though by less, while the
pseudo-passive slope is at least as steep as the passive slope. The trends look much the same for
male and female agents, although in English the active-by-affectedness interaction differs
between them. The design therefore balances the two agent genders across participants
(Appendix B).

*Note.* Panels are by language across rows and by agent gender across columns. Points are
individual pilot ratings, jittered. Lines are linear trends for each sentence type, with 95%
confidence bands that ignore the clustering of ratings within participants and verbs and so
understate the uncertainty. Affectedness is the score normed for each agent-gender version,
z-scored within language, and the model uses one score per verb, the mean of the two. The
Norwegian materials include no pseudo-passive.

`\vspace{12pt}`{=latex}

# Design-Analysis Method

The design analysis simulates many studies and analyses each one as the real data will be
analysed. Simulations of single languages, from the cumulative-logit model planned for each
language's data, show how precisely one language's data estimate each interaction. Simulations of
`r K_PLAN` to `r max(K_MORE)` languages then evaluate the confirmatory test, which combines the per-language
estimates in the way described below. The procedure stays within the Bayesian framework
throughout, because the confirmatory test is a Bayes factor. Its result is therefore the
probability that a study reaches a Bayes factor of 10, a different quantity from the power to
return a significant *p*-value.

The per-language simulations take their effects from the pilot. For each language, the planned
model is fitted to the pilot ratings. On every simulated study, the fixed effects and ordinal
thresholds are drawn together from one draw of that fit's posterior, and the random-effect
covariance is held at its posterior mean. New participants and new verb deviations are then drawn
around the pilot's own verbs and their measured affectedness scores. The simulated studies thus
range over the effect sizes the pilot leaves plausible, which allows for the uncertainty of a
single pilot's point estimate [@albersLakens2018]. Every pilot
language goes forward whatever its pilot showed, so the follow-up bias that Albers and Lakens
describe does not arise.

Published effect sizes are subject to publication bias and tend to overstate true effects
[@gelmanCarlin2014; @button2013], so design analyses anchored to them can be optimistic
[@vasishth2018]. In this report, published estimates enter only the multi-language synthesis,
where they join the pilot estimates in estimating the population from which the simulated
languages are drawn. Their average, `r mnum2(kpop("glossa_protocol", "mean_effect"))` per
standard deviation of affectedness, is close to the three pilots'
`r mnum2(kpop("claps_protocol", "mean_effect"))`, so they show no sign of inflation relative to
the CLAPS protocol. Like the pilot data, the published data serve only to plan the study. Neither
will enter the confirmatory tests, which will use only new data collected under the registered
protocol.

Affectedness is a property of the verb. In the study, it will be rated in a separate norming task,
in which twenty further speakers of each language rate the affectedness of the patient in each
event, once for each agent-gender version. A verb's score is the mean of its two version scores,
so each verb carries one affectedness score, the same across participants and sentence types.
Every affectedness effect is therefore estimated from differences between verbs, and the verbs
and the spread of their scores bound its precision, however many participants take part. This is
the stimulus-sampling limit long recognised in psycholinguistics [@clark1973] and quantified for
designs with crossed random effects by Westfall et al. [-@westfallKennyJudd2014; see also
@brysbaertStevens2018; @juddWestfallKenny2017]. With unlimited participants, the standard error of
such an effect cannot fall below the by-verb standard deviation of that effect divided by the
square root of the verbs' summed squared affectedness deviations. That floor can be read from the
fitted pilot models without simulation.

The analysis model has the maximal random-effects structure the design supports
[@barrLevyScheepersTily2013], with correlated by-participant slopes for sentence type,
affectedness and their interaction, and by-verb intercepts and sentence-type slopes. Because
affectedness does not vary within a verb, a by-verb affectedness slope cannot be estimated and is
omitted. Affectedness is centred and divided by twice its standard deviation within each language,
and effects are reported per standard deviation of affectedness. The priors are centred at zero on
the focal slopes, so they favour neither sign. The affectedness slope and the active interaction
take normal priors with a standard deviation of 0.5 on the model's scale, or 0.25 per standard
deviation of affectedness, and the pseudo-passive interaction takes 0.6, or 0.30 per standard
deviation. The other fixed effects take normal priors with a standard deviation of 1.5. The
ordinal thresholds take Student-*t* priors with three degrees of freedom and a scale of 2.5, and
the random-effect standard deviations Student-*t* priors with three degrees of freedom and a scale
of 1. Their correlations take an LKJ prior with a shape of 2 [@gelman2006;
@lewandowskiKurowickaJoe2009].

In the confirmatory test, each language is first analysed on its own with this model, so it keeps
its own rating thresholds, participants and verbs. A verb's
effects are therefore estimated separately in each language. This suits verbs whose translations
mean similar but never identical things, and across the meta-analysis languages verb effects
correlate only about 0.2. The per-language posterior means and standard deviations of each
interaction are then combined in a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis, with language as the
random effect. The mean across languages takes a normal prior with the standard deviation of the
per-language prior, and the between-language standard deviation, $\tau$, a half-normal prior with
a scale of 0.5. One- and two-stage analyses of data from many studies give very similar results
when each study is large and both make the same modelling assumptions [@burkeEnsorRiley2017],
and each language here contributes 80 participants and about 72 verbs. A single model across all languages proved hard to fit (see
Limitations), so it is kept as a planned robustness check, reported beside the confirmatory test
but deciding neither hypothesis.

Evidence for each hypothesis is a one-sided Bayes factor against the null hypothesis that the
mean across languages is zero, with the languages free to vary around the mean under both
hypotheses. The hypothesis is represented by the half of the zero-centred prior on the predicted
side, a half-normal distribution of the kind *Nature Human Behaviour* names for representing a
prediction [@dienes2014], and the null by a mean of exactly zero. The Bayes factor is the
Savage–Dickey ratio of the prior and posterior densities of the mean at zero
[@wagenmakersLodewyckxKuriyalGrasman2010], multiplied by twice the posterior probability that the
mean is negative [@moreyWagenmakers2014]. A Bayes factor of 1/10 or less is therefore strong
evidence for no effect, and an effect in the other direction counts towards it. A simulated study
counts as a detection when its Bayes factor reaches 10.

Each stimulus exists in two versions, one with a woman agent and one with a man agent. Each
participant will see one version of each verb, so an English or Turkish session has
`r gv_trials("English") / 2` sentences, and the simulations describe that session. The versions
are balanced across participants by counterbalanced lists (Appendix B).

The per-language simulations comprise `r da_reps` simulated studies at each of
`r and_list(da_ns)` participants per language. The studies keep the pilot's verb counts,
`r ppv("English", "n_verbs")` in English and Turkish and `r ppv("Norwegian", "n_verbs")` in
Norwegian. Each study is fitted with four chains of 3,000 iterations at a target acceptance rate of
.99 and a maximum treedepth of 12. After 1,000 warm-up iterations per chain, 8,000 post-warm-up
draws remain. The confirmatory analysis will use sixteen chains of 5,000 iterations with 2,000 of
warm-up. These simulations serve to check the normal approximation with which the simulations of
`r K_PLAN` languages represent each language's estimate (see Limitations).

The simulations ran on the University of Oxford's Advanced Research Computing service under R
4.4.2, with brms 2.21.0 and the cmdstanr backend on CmdStan 2.39.0, and the lockfile `renv.lock`
fixes the package versions. The analysis code, the simulation settings and the aggregated results
are openly available at <https://github.com/pablobernabeu/CLAPS-analysis>, where H1 and H2 carry the
labels h1b and h2b. The registered analysis itself is in the repository's `stage2` folder, as
numbered scripts with the order in which they will be run. This report rebuilds from those results
without the raw pilot data, which are not yet public.

# Results

## The Pilot Estimates

@tbl-pilot-estimates gives the two interactions in each pilot language, from the planned model
fitted to the pilot ratings. The active interaction runs in the predicted direction in all three
languages, most weakly in Turkish. The pseudo-passive interaction runs in the predicted direction in
English but the other way in Turkish, where the affectedness slope is steeper for pseudo-passives
than for passives. The simulations draw the Turkish effect from that posterior and so inherit the
reversal. By contrast, the per-language models of the meta-analysis show the negative
pseudo-passive interaction in Balinese, Indonesian and Mandarin.

```{r tbl-pilot-estimates}
#| tbl-cap: "Pilot Estimates of the Two Interactions"

# From scripts/summarise_pilot_interactions.R, which reads the pilot posterior draws, so
# the public copy of this report needs only the summary.
pint <- read_csv("../outputs/design_summary_pilot/pilot_interactions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pe <- pint |>
  mutate(language = lang_factor(language),
         Estimate = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", snum2(per_sd_mean), snum2(per_sd_lo95),
                            snum2(per_sd_hi95))) |>
  select(language, hypothesis, Estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = hypothesis, values_from = Estimate, values_fill = "--") |>
  arrange(language) |>
  rename(Language = language, `H1, active` = H1, `H2, pseudo-passive` = H2)
kable(pe, align = "lrr")
```

`\vspace{-8pt}`{=latex}

*Note.* Posterior means with 95% credible intervals, in logits per standard deviation of
affectedness. Both interactions are predicted to be negative. The Norwegian materials include no
pseudo-passive.

`\vspace{12pt}`{=latex}

## The Confirmatory Pooled Test

The protocol sets a minimum of `r K_PLAN` languages, and the collaborators hope for 30 or more, so
the confirmatory test is simulated with `r K_PLAN` languages and with `r and_list(K_MORE)`. In
earlier studies, about three quarters of the languages had a pseudo-passive, so H2 is simulated
with `r K_PLAN_PP` languages, and with `r and_list(k_pp(K_MORE))` respectively. Which languages
will take part is not yet known, so the simulations do not assume that any of the seven measured
so far, the three CLAPS pilots and the four other meta-analysis languages, is among them. Instead,
every language's effect is drawn from a population whose mean and between-language spread are held
at their estimates from those seven (the posterior mean and median), as in a conventional power
analysis. Each language's estimate is simulated at the precision that 80 participants and 72 verbs
achieve, and each simulated study is analysed as registered. For H2, the population is estimated
from the `r num_word(n_measured_pp)` measured languages with a pseudo-passive.

On these assumptions, the pooled test of H1 reaches a Bayes factor of 10 in
`r pct_r(kreg_rate("H1"))` of `r format(unique(kpoint$n_reps), big.mark = ",")` simulated studies
(95% Monte Carlo interval `r kreg_ci("H1")`), and the pooled test of H2 in
`r pct_r(kreg_rate("H2"))` (`r kreg_ci("H2")`). The rates rise with the number of languages: to
`r more_rates("H1")[1]` for H1 and `r more_rates("H2")[1]` for H2 with `r K_MORE[1]` languages,
`r more_rates("H1")[2]` and `r more_rates("H2")[2]` with `r K_MORE[2]`, and
`r more_rates("H1")[3]` and `r more_rates("H2")[3]` with `r K_MORE[3]`. With 60 verbs in every
language, the fewest the protocol allows, no rate falls by as much as a percentage point. No study
at the estimated effects ends with strong evidence for the null, a Bayes factor of 1/10 or less.
In studies with no effect, a mean of zero with the estimated spread, a Bayes factor of 10 arises in
`r null_rate("H1")` of studies for H1 and `r null_rate("H2")` for H2, which is the rate of
misleading evidence [@schonbrodtWagenmakers2018]. Allowing for uncertainty about the mean and spread
as well, by drawing them from their posterior in each simulated study, the rates with `r K_PLAN`
languages are `r pct_r(kreg_rate("H1", tab = kunc))` for H1 and
`r pct_r(kreg_rate("H2", tab = kunc))` for H2, since the seven measured languages leave some
chance that the mean effect is small.

# The Sampling Plan

Every team will collect usable data from 80 participants, replacing any participant who is
excluded. The number is fixed in advance because each team must state its sample size to its
ethics committee. Each language will use as close to 72 verbs as its supply of suitable verbs
allows. Every language enters the pooled tests whatever its pilot showed, Turkish included, since
leaving a language out on the strength of its pilot would amount to choosing languages by their
results. The H2 rates above already allow for the Turkish reversal, since Turkish is one of the
`r num_word(n_measured_pp)` languages behind its population. @tbl-design summarises the
planned analyses and their detection rates.

*Nature Human Behaviour* sets its 0.95 power requirement for frequentist analysis plans. For a
Bayesian plan, it asks that data collection continue until the Bayes factor is "at least 10 times in
favour of the experimental hypothesis over the null hypothesis (or vice versa)". Authors with
limited resources may instead state a maximum feasible sample, "sufficiently large that
inconclusive results at this sample size would nevertheless be an important message for the
field". CLAPS takes the second route for both hypotheses. Each team stops at 80 participants, the
most the collecting teams can provide, and data collection closes six months after the minimum of
`r K_PLAN` languages is reached, whatever the Bayes factors. A test whose Bayes factor has reached neither 10 nor 1/10 by then is reported as inconclusive. At
that sample, each language is close to the limit its verbs set, so further participants would add
little. An inconclusive result from at least `r K_PLAN` languages and
`r format(80 * K_PLAN, big.mark = ",")` participants would still be an important message for the
field.

# Limitations

At 80 participants, no simulated per-language fit has a divergent transition or a saturated
treedepth. Confirmatory fits must also reach an R-hat below 1.01 and bulk and tail effective sample
sizes of at least 400. With the shorter runs used for simulation, `r da("English", 80, "n_converged")`
of `r da_reps` English fits meet those thresholds, as do `r da("Norwegian", 80, "n_converged")`
Norwegian and `r da("Turkish", 80, "n_converged")` Turkish fits. The fits that met them gave the
same results as the others, within what random subsets of their size would show. With longer
chains and four times as many of them, the confirmatory fits will have six times the post-warm-up
draws.

<!-- The figures in the next paragraph are typed, because their source stays on the
     cluster: the pooled refit of 20-27 August 2026 (job 8614954, model level
     L5_cross_verbblock_aligned), saved as pilot_fit_pooled_aligned.rds. Its log gives
     75,528 observations over 210 verbs and 6,000 of 8,000 transitions at the maximum
     treedepth. Its 8,000 draws of the active interaction give a mean of -0.484 and a 95%
     interval from -1.014 to 0.297 on the model's scale, which times 0.5036, the mean pilot
     SD of the scaled predictor, is -0.244 [-0.510, +0.150] per SD. Checked on 9 October
     2026. -->

Fitted to the combined pilot data, 75,528 ratings over 210 verbs, a single model across languages
estimated the interaction at about $-0.24$ logits per standard deviation of affectedness, with a
95% credible interval from $-0.51$ to $+0.15$. That is close to the average of the three pilot
estimates, `r mnum2(mean(pp$interaction_per_sd))`, but the model is much harder to fit than the
per-language ones. It saturated the maximum treedepth on three quarters of its iterations, a
problem longer chains do not fix. In simulations with `r K_LADDER_SIM` languages of 20 verbs each, no
form more complex than one with sentence-type slopes for participants and verbs and uncorrelated
by-language slopes converged. The robustness check's model ladder is therefore expected to end at
that form.

The `r K_PLAN`-language figures rest on an assumed population of languages. The seven measured so
far are a convenience sample from five families in two macroareas, and the simulations treat
every language as a draw from a population like them. They also give each language's estimate the
standard error of a normal approximation to its analysis. The calibration behind the rates for a
language without a pilot widens that standard error by a factor of `r num2(kreg_shift$k)`, and
with it no rate with `r K_PLAN` languages falls by more than
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * kreg_shift$max_fall)` percentage points.

Every pilot participant saw both versions of every verb, whereas in the study itself each
participant will see one version of each verb (Appendix B). The Norwegian materials include no

`\vspace{12pt}`{=latex}

{{< pagebreak >}}

```{=latex}
% Appendix tables carry their own letter, as APA 7 asks, so the body
% sequence is not interrupted by tables the reader meets later.
\setcounter{table}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{B\arabic{table}}
\begin{center}
{\large\bfseries Appendix B}\\[3pt]
{\bfseries The Agent-Gender Lists}
\end{center}
```

This appendix sets out how the two agent-gender versions of each stimulus are balanced across
participants, and why. Each participant will see one version of each verb, so the balance has to
come from the assignment of versions to participants.

The versions need balancing because agent gender moves the interaction in English. A linear mixed
model of the 1-to-7 pilot ratings, used here only to gauge the relative size of the gender term, codes agent
gender as plus or minus a half. In it, the English interaction is
`r mnum2(gv_per_sd(gvev("English", GV_TERM_H1B, "h1b_estimate")))` rating points per standard
deviation of affectedness, and its gender-by-active-by-affectedness term is
`r snum3(gv_per_sd(gvev("English", GV_TERM_H1B)))` (*SE* =
`r num3(gv_per_sd(gvev("English", GV_TERM_H1B, "se")))`). The interaction is therefore markedly
stronger for man-agent items than for woman-agent ones. A design in which every participant saw
only woman-agent versions, or only man-agent ones, would move the English interaction by about
`r pct0(gv_shift("English"))`, against `r pct0(gv_shift("Turkish"))` in Turkish and
`r pct0(gv_shift("Norwegian"))` in Norwegian.

Counterbalanced lists remove that shift without lengthening the session. Each list shows woman
agents on half the verbs and man agents on the other half, with the same agent across a verb's
sentence types, and across the lists each verb appears equally often with each agent. Each
participant therefore sees both agent genders equally often, each verb is rated in each version by
half the sample, and the estimand remains the slope averaged over agent gender. The protocol uses
eight such lists, although two would be enough. With two, the verbs would be split into two sets
of `r ppv("English", "n_verbs") / 2`, or `r ppv("Norwegian", "n_verbs") / 2` in Norwegian, matched
on affectedness and verb class. One list would show the first set with woman agents and the second
with man agents, and the other the reverse. As long as every list shows both agent genders on
matched verb sets, unequal numbers of participants across the lists leave the interaction
essentially unchanged. Even so, assigning participants to the lists in turn, and replacing
exclusions within the same list, keeps each verb's two versions evenly rated. Splitting the
agent-gender versions across participants in this way follows Ambridge et al.
[-@ambridgeBidgoodPineRowlandFreudenthal2016, Study 3] and the Hebrew study of Ambridge et al.
[-@ambridgeArnonBekman2023].

Both agent-gender versions should stay in the affectedness rating task, which asks for one
judgement per verb and agent gender and is short. Halving it would leave each agent-specific score
resting on half as many raters and would attenuate every slope estimated from those scores.
